issue: Does the joint participant exception to the spousal testimonial privilege survive Trammel v. United States, or should a spouse who is a co-participant in the charged crime be compellable to testify against the defendant-spouse?
provision: Trammel v. United States, 445 U.S. 40 (1980); Fed. R. Evid. 501

sides.position: The joint participant exception does not survive Trammel; a spouse who participated in the crime may be compelled to testify.
cases: United States v. Pineda-Mateo, 905 F.3d 13 (1st Cir. 2018)
In re Grand Jury Subpoena, 755 F.2d 1022 (2d Cir. 1985)
In re Grand Jury, 633 F.2d 276 (3d Cir. 1980)
United States v. Ramos-Oseguera, 120 F.3d 1028 (9th Cir. 1997)
United States v. Diggs, 81 F.4th 755 (7th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: The joint participant exception to the spousal testimonial privilege remains good law in this circuit.
cases: United States v. Van Drunen, 501 F.2d 1393 (7th Cir. 1974)

this_court: The excerpts come from a separate writing that urges abandoning the joint participant exception and says the court is isolated; the excerpts do not show the majority's holding, so this court's formal position is not established.
quote: That leaves our court isolated on the short end of a lopsided circuit split.
cite: United States v. Tobias Diggs, 81 F.4th 755 (7th Cir. 2023)
